summary: Indian regulators can levy environmental compensation on industrial units whose pollution load exceeds permitted limits, scaled by the size of the unit, the severity of the pollution, and how long it continues. Compensation is a polluter-pays instrument, so a longer period of excess emissions increases exposure.

topic: Carbon credit trading (successor to PAT energy certificates)
summary: India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS), administered by the Bureau of Energy Efficiency, is gradually replacing the Perform, Achieve and Trade (PAT) energy-efficiency scheme for notified sectors, which include pulp and paper and cement. Covered entities have legally binding emissions-intensity targets, measured in tonnes of CO2e per unit of product. Entities that beat their target can earn tradable Carbon Credit Certificates, and those that miss it must buy certificates. A degrading machine that raises emissions per unit of product therefore reduces credit earnings or increases the number of certificates a plant must buy.
source_name: Bureau of Energy Efficiency, Carbon Credit Trading Scheme; ICAP summary of the Indian CCTS
